newsitem.title: USA: U.S. home mortgage rates up in week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. home mortgage rates up in week.

text.p: U.S. home mortgage rates rose this week as Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks revived inflation concerns, Freddie Mac said on Thursday.
Thirty-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 7.84 percent, up from 7.65 percent last week, while 15-year rates climbed to 7.35 percent from 7.15 percent.
One-year adjustable mortgage rates also rose to 5.54 percent from 5.49 percent last week, it said.
A year ago, the 30-year loan rate averaged 7.38 percent, the 15-year 6.87 percent and the adjustable loan 5.40 percent.

"As expected, interest rates rose considerably after Greenspan warned the financial markets to exercise caution last week," said Frank Nothaft, deputy chief economist for Freddie Mac, which recently changed its name from the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp.
Nothaft added that it is very likely "rates will continue to rise over the next few weeks."
Greenspan on Wednesday gave the second leg of his semi-annual economic testimony to Congress, leaving many economists and traders expecting a Fed rate hike soon.

Lenders charged an average of 1.7 percent in fees and points on both 30- and 15-year loans, unchanged from last week. They charged 1.4 percent on adjustable mortgages, also unchanged from the prior week.
Freddie Mac is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
